# Data wrangling {#sec-m1-manipulacao}

From here on we use the course's real dataset: the **TKU of coastal shipping** (ANTAQ,
2025), with 732 records of pairs of port facilities. TKU (*tonelada-quilômetro útil*) is the
cargo tonnage times the distance carried, in tonne-km. The file is listed in
[Example data](a-dados.qmd) and is in the repository, in `dados/`.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(stringr)
```

## Reading

### Spreadsheets

```{r}
bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx")
dim(bruto)
names(bruto)
```

Look at the name of the last column: `TKU\n(t x km)`, with a line break and brackets. Names
like this force you to write `` `TKU\n(t x km)` `` with backticks in every reference. The
first thing to do with any spreadsheet is to standardise the names:

```{r}
bruto |> janitor::clean_names() |> names()
```

`janitor::clean_names()` turns everything into lower case, replaces spaces and punctuation with `_` and
removes accents. The names become usable, but are still long. Since we know the structure of the
file, we will set short names **by position**, guarded by a check. If ANTAQ
changes the number of columns in the next release, the script stops instead of renaming wrongly.
The new names are year, cargo profile, HS2 commodity group, then country, state, city and
facility of origin and of destination, and the TKU:

```{r}
colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

base <- bruto
stopifnot(ncol(base) == length(colunas))
names(base) <- colunas

dplyr::glimpse(base)
```

Still at this stage, a filter worth explaining: **132 of the 732 records have TKU equal to
zero**. They are combinations of commodity and cargo profile with no flow in the period, published
as empty rows with `-` in the identification fields. They are analysed in detail in
@sec-m1-limpeza; here we just set them aside.

```{r}
base |> dplyr::count(tem_fluxo = tku > 0)

base <- base |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0)
nrow(base)
```

If you prefer to rename by the original name, explicitly:

```{r}
#| eval: false
base <- bruto |>
  dplyr::rename(
    ano           = Ano,
    perfil        = `Perfil da Carga`,
    sh2           = `Grupo de Mercadoria (SH2)`,
    uf_origem     = `UF de Origem`,
    cidade_origem = `Cidade de Origem`,
    tku           = `TKU\n(t x km)`
  )
```

Other useful arguments of `read_excel()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", sheet = "Dados")        # sheet by name
readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", skip = 3)               # skips decorative header rows
readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", n_max = 1000)           # only the first rows (for inspection)
readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", col_types = "text")     # reads everything as text (avoids coercion)
readxl::read_excel("arquivo.xlsx", na = c("", "-", "n/d")) # what should become NA
```

### Text files

```{r}
csv <- readr::read_csv("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(csv)
names(csv) |> head(4)
```

For files in the Brazilian format, with `;` as separator and a decimal comma, use `read_csv2()`.
Give the *encoding* when the file comes from a legacy system:

```{r}
#| eval: false
readr::read_csv2("arquivo.csv", locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1"))
```

### Large files: `duckplyr`

`readr` and `read_excel` load everything into memory. When the file has millions of rows
(GTFS, GPS data, toll records, routing matrices), it is worth using `duckplyr`, which
runs the query in **DuckDB** and brings only the result into memory.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(duckplyr)

# reading is "lazy": nothing is loaded yet
grande <- duckplyr::read_csv_duckdb("dados/roteamento_milhoes.csv")

resultado <- grande |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_destino == "PR") |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE), .by = uf_origem) |>
  dplyr::collect()          # only here is the query run
```

The syntax is the same as `dplyr`; the difference is `collect()` at the end, which materialises the
result. In module 3 we compare the processing time of the two approaches with
`system.time()` on a routing dataset.

::: {.callout-note}
## Which package to use

| Situation | Tool |
|:--|:--|
| Up to ~1 million rows, code other people will read | `dplyr` |
| Files that do not fit in memory, queries with filters and aggregation | `duckplyr` / `duckdb` |
| Intensive wrangling with many operations per group | `data.table` |

The three live together in the same script: it is common to read with `duckplyr`, aggregate, `collect()` and carry on
in `dplyr`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## About `data.table`

`data.table` is generally **faster** than `dplyr` for heavy wrangling (many
`group_by`s, tables with tens of millions of rows). The reason it is not this course's main package
is teaching, not technical: its syntax (`DT[i, j, by]`, with unquoted column references
and operators such as `:=`) is more compact but less readable for people who are
learning. If after the course you decide to move a whole script to `data.table` for
performance, any AI assistant (@sec-m1-ambiente) reliably converts a `dplyr` snippet to
`data.table`, because it is a mechanical translation between equivalent syntaxes.
Check the result against the same anchor totals as in the previous chapter.
:::

## The `dplyr` verbs

### `select()`: choose columns

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::select(uf_origem, uf_destino, tku) |>
  head(3)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
dplyr::select(base, tidyr::starts_with("uf"))          # by prefix
dplyr::select(base, tidyr::contains("cidade"))         # by part of the name
dplyr::select(base, -pais_origem, -pais_destino)  # remove
dplyr::select(base, carga = perfil)    # select and rename
dplyr::select(base, dplyr::where(is.numeric))          # by type
```

### `filter()`: choose rows

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_destino == "PR") |>
  nrow()

base |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_origem == "AM", tku > 1e9) |>          # the comma means "and"
  dplyr::select(cidade_origem, uf_destino, tku)

base |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_destino %in% c("PR", "SC", "RS")) |>   # South region
  nrow()

base |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(perfil, "Granel")) |>
  dplyr::count(perfil)
```

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_origem != uf_destino) |>               # excludes flows within a state
  nrow()
```

### `mutate()`: create and change columns

```{r}
base <- base |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    tku_bi   = tku / 1e9,
    ligacao  = stringr::str_c(uf_origem, " > ", uf_destino),
    interestadual = uf_origem != uf_destino,
    faixa = dplyr::case_when(
      tku >= 1e9 ~ "alto",
      tku >= 1e6 ~ "médio",
      .default   = "baixo"
    )
  )

base |> dplyr::select(ligacao, tku_bi, faixa) |> head(4)
```

### `arrange()`: sort

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku)) |>
  dplyr::select(ligacao, cidade_origem, cidade_destino, tku_bi) |>
  head(5)
```

### `summarise()` and grouping

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    ligacoes = dplyr::n(),
    tku_total = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE),
    tku_medio = mean(tku, na.rm = TRUE),
    tku_max   = max(tku, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Grouping is the most used operation of all. The modern syntax uses the `.by` argument:

```{r}
por_uf_destino <- base |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    ligacoes  = dplyr::n(),
    tku_bi    = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9,
    .by = uf_destino
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi))

por_uf_destino |> head(10)
```

The equivalent with `group_by()`, which you will see in older material:

```{r}
#| eval: false
base |>
  dplyr::group_by(uf_destino) |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

Grouping by more than one variable, with a percentage share:

```{r}
base |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(perfil, uf_destino)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = tku / sum(tku), .by = perfil) |>
  dplyr::filter(part > 0.10) |>
  dplyr::arrange(perfil, dplyr::desc(part))
```

Note that `mutate(..., .by = ...)` computes **within the group without collapsing the table**. It
works like a calculated field in a pivot table.

### `count()`, `distinct()`, `slice_max()`

```{r}
base |> dplyr::count(perfil, sort = TRUE)
base |> dplyr::distinct(uf_origem) |> nrow()
base |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 3) |> dplyr::select(ligacao, tku_bi)
base |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 1, by = uf_destino) |> dplyr::select(uf_destino, ligacao, tku_bi) |> head(5)
```

## Reshaping: *long* ↔ *wide*

Tables for human reading are **wide** (one column per category); tables for analysis and
charts are **long** (one row per observation). `tidyr` converts between the two forms.

### *Long to wide*: the OD matrix

```{r}
od_longo <- base |>
  dplyr::filter(uf_origem != uf_destino) |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, .by = c(uf_origem, uf_destino))

head(od_longo, 4)

od_largo <- od_longo |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = uf_destino,
    values_from = tku_bi,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(uf_origem)

od_largo
```

This is exactly the structure of an **origin–destination matrix**, ready to export to
Excel or convert into a `matrix`:

```{r}
m <- as.matrix(od_largo[, -1])
rownames(m) <- od_largo$uf_origem
round(m[1:5, 1:5], 2)
```

### *Wide to long*: back to the analytical form

```{r}
od_largo |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -uf_origem,
    names_to  = "uf_destino",
    values_to = "tku_bi"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku_bi > 0) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) |>
  head(5)
```

A frequent case with SIDRA and Census data: several year columns that should be a single
`ano` (year) column.

```{r}
pop <- data.frame(
  municipio = c("Paranaguá", "Santos"),
  pop_2010  = c(140469, 419400),
  pop_2022  = c(156174, 418375)
)

pop |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = tidyr::starts_with("pop_"),
    names_to = "ano",
    names_prefix = "pop_",
    names_transform = list(ano = as.integer),
    values_to = "populacao"
  )
```

## Exporting results

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE)

# CSV in the international standard (decimal point)
readr::write_csv(por_uf_destino, "resultados/tku_por_uf_destino.csv")

# CSV to open in Excel set to Portuguese (semicolon, decimal comma)
readr::write_csv2(por_uf_destino, "resultados/tku_por_uf_destino_excel.csv")

# Excel, with one sheet per table
writexl::write_xlsx(
  list(
    "TKU por UF" = por_uf_destino,
    "Matriz OD"  = od_largo
  ),
  "resultados/cabotagem_2025.xlsx"
)

# R's native format: keeps types exactly
saveRDS(base, "resultados/cabotagem_limpa.rds")
base2 <- readRDS("resultados/cabotagem_limpa.rds")

# Open and efficient format, to exchange with Python/QGIS
arrow::write_parquet(base, "resultados/cabotagem.parquet")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which format to deliver

- **Excel (`.xlsx`)**: when the recipient will open and read it. Use named sheets.
- **CSV**: when the file feeds another system. Agree on the separator first.
- **RDS**: between steps of your own workflow. Fast and with no loss of types.
- **Parquet**: large datasets shared between tools.
- In the following modules come `.gpkg` and `.shp`, for spatial data.
:::
